blocks.text: Reactions of Group 2 Oxides, Hydroxides & Carbonates
Reactions of Group 2 oxides with water

blocks.md:
- All Group 2 oxides are **basic**, except for BeO which is **amphoteric **(it can act both as an acid and base)
- Group 2 oxides react with water to form **alkaline **solutions which generally get more **alkaline** going down the group

  - This happens because the hydroxides that form become more soluble as you move down the group
  - This means that more hydroxide ions, OH<sup>–</sup>, dissociate into the solution causing the pH to increase

blocks.text: Group 2 oxide reactions with the water table

blocks.md:
| **Group 2 oxide** | **Reaction with water** | **Observations** |
|---|---|---|
| **MgO** | MgO (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) | MgO is only slightly soluble in water, therefore a weakly alkaline solution (pH 10.0) is formed |
| **CaO** | CaO (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) | A vigorous reaction which releases a lot of energy, causing some of the water to boil off as the solid lump seems to expand and open (pH 11.0) |
| **SrO** | SrO (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> (aq) |   |
| **BaO** | BaO (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> (aq) |   |
- Remember that:
**oxide + water → hydroxide**
- And that a solution of calcium hydroxide is called **limewater**

blocks.text: Reactions of Group 2 metals with acid

blocks.md:
- The Group 2 metals will react with dilute acids to form **colourless solutions of metal salts **

  - For example, they will form colourless solutions of metal chlorides if reacted with hydrochloric acid
- When metals react with an acid, the by-product of this reaction is hydrogen gas

blocks.text: Group 2 reactions with dilute acids table

blocks.md:
| **Group 2 element** | **Reaction with dilute HCl** | **Reaction with dilute H**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4**</sub> |
|---|---|---|
| **Mg** | Mg (s) + 2HCl (aq) → MgCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) | Mg (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → MgSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) |
| **Ca** | Ca (s) + 2HCl (aq) → CaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) | Ca (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → CaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) |
| **Sr** | Sr (s) + 2HCl (aq) → SrCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) | Sr (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → SrSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) |
| **Ba** | Ba (s) + 2HCl (aq) → BaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) | Ba (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → BaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) |

- When some Group 2 metals react with sulfuric acid rather than hydrochloric, an insoluble sulfate forms
- Going down the group, the Group 2 sulfates become less and less soluble

  - Calcium sulfate is sparingly soluble, but strontium sulfate and barium sulfate are insoluble

blocks.text: Reactions of Group 2 oxides with acid

blocks.md:
- Group 2 sulfates also form when a Group 2 oxide is reacted with an acid
- The **insoluble sulfates **form at the **surface **of the oxide, which means that the solid oxide beneath it can’t react with the acid
- This can be prevented to an extent by using the oxide in **powder **form and **stirring**, in which case neutralisation can take place
- Remember that:
**metal oxide + dilute hydrochloric acid → salt + water**
**metal oxide + dilute sulfuric acid → sulfate + water**

- The Group 2 metal hydroxides form **colourless solutions of metal chlorides **when they react with a dilute acid
- The sulfates decrease in **solubility **going down the group (barium sulfate is an insoluble white precipitate)

blocks.text: Group 2 hydroxide reactions with dilute acids table

blocks.md:
| **Group 2 hydroxide** | **Reaction with dilute HCl** | **Reaction with dilute H**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4**</sub> |
|---|---|---|
| **Mg(OH)**<sub>**2**</sub> | Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + 2HCl (aq) → MgCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) | Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → MgSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) |
| **Ca(OH)**<sub>**2**</sub> | Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + 2HCl (aq) → CaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) | Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → CaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) |
| **Sr(OH)**<sub>**2**</sub> | Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + 2HCl (aq) → SrCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) | Sr(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → SrSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) |
| **Ba(OH)**<sub>**2**</sub> | Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + 2HCl (aq) → BaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) | Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → BaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) |
- Remember that:
**metal hydroxide + dilute acid → salt + water**
**metal hydroxide + dilute sulfuric acid → sulfate + water**

- All Group 2 carbonates (except for **BeCO**<sub>**3**</sub>) are **insoluble in water**
- All Group 2 carbonates will form **soluble chloride salts, **water and carbon dioxide gas when reacted with dilute hydrochloric acid
- When reacted with sulfuric acid, the carbonates of Ca, Sr and Ba form an **insoluble sulfate layer **on their surface which **stops **any further reaction after the initial bubbling (**effervescence) of carbon dioxide gas **is seen

blocks.text: Group 2 carbonate reactions with dilute acids

blocks.md:
| **Group 2 carbonate** | **Reaction with dilute HCl** | **Reaction with dilute H**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4**</sub> |
|---|---|---|
| **MgCO**<sub>**3**</sub> | MgCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + 2HCl (aq) → MgCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | MgCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → MgSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) |
| **CaCO**<sub>**3**</sub> | CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + 2HCl (aq) → CaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → CaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) |
| **SrCO**<sub>**3**</sub> | SrCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + 2HCl (aq) → SrCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | SrCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → SrSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) |
| **BaCO**<sub>**3**</sub> | BaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + 2HCl (aq) → BaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | BaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → BaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g) |
- Remember that:
**metal carbonate + dilute hydrochloric acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide**
**metal carbonate + dilute sulfuric acid → sulfate + water + carbon dioxide**
